problem_framing.reason: A1 lists options, including channel partnership and adjacent segments. Alternatives 2 and 3 are effectively the same, so the list is partly redundant. It states the objective but does not separate the underlying goal (capturing value from individual buyers) from the suggested product solution. It does not note that 'differentiated proposition' need not mean a new product line. The €20,000 / 12-week constraint does not appear in the case packet and cannot be verified from the supplied material.

causal_mechanism.reason: A9 names who changes behaviour (creators wanting to be taken seriously) and why (credibility signalling), plus premium-price capture. The chain does not explain why this requires a differentiated line rather than the existing professional range. A19 then contradicts it: the line is 'lower price point' for 'price-sensitive' buyers, yet is meant to 'capture premium pricing'. That falls short of a full chain.

distinct_theories.reason: T2 (A10) is a near-verbatim copy of T1 (A9). It has the same mechanism, the same value capture and identical predictions. No rival theory is offered, for example that the existing professional range already serves home buyers as an upgrade path.

assumptions_predictions.reason: A9's predictions are observable: purchase intent or willingness to pay, and credibility rankings. However, the willingness-to-pay comparison is against a 'generic consumer line', not against the single professional range. Failure would therefore not threaten the choice the question actually asks about.

evidence_judgement.reason: A11 and A12 label positive reception of tutorial videos (a company claim) as support for a purchase theory, while their own 'does not show' text admits it does not. A14 labels the 2018 market-share figure as support for T1. It ignores the 2018 date and does not note that A15's later source reports a pandemic-driven drop and re-stabilisation. The 'does not show' text is boilerplate repeated across sources. The MusicRadar upgrade observation (found in A5 and A8), which bears directly on whether one professional range already serves home buyers, is never assessed.

seeking_challenge.reason: A13 searches against T1, but the result is then logged as supporting T1 (A14). The decline evidence (A15, A16) is marked neutral rather than engaged as a challenge to demand. The episode does not report fairly what it found against the theory, nor whether it found nothing.

experiment_design.reason: A17 assigns T2 the opposite prediction, even though T2's own stated predictions in A10 are identical to T1's. The contrast is manufactured, so the test cannot separate the stated theories. It compares against a generic consumer proposition rather than the existing professional range. The decision rule leaves a gap between 0% and 15% and is restated inconsistently in A19. Stated intent cannot settle market size, despite A19's claim that it will.

revision.reason: Revision is excluded from packet.applicable_dimensions, and no update was scheduled.

recommendation.reason: A19 commits to developing the line before any test, rating T1 'likely' on evidence the assessments themselves say does not show demand. The value proposition is internally contradictory (lower price versus premium capture). One reversal condition contradicts A17's decision rule. The other separates 'brand reputation' from 'perceived professional standard', which T1 itself equates.

red_flags.reason: Reception of tutorial videos is treated as support for creators buying Neumann products at a premium. This is a marketing claim used as evidence of demand.
Home-studio share of category revenue in 2018 is labelled as support for a credibility-driven purchase theory. The source does not address that theory, and later evidence of decline (A15) is ignored.
T1 is rated 'likely' and the line is recommended despite no supporting evidence of willingness to pay. The claim that the survey 'will resolve' market size is also unsupported.

T1 and T2 are copies with identical predictions. The opposing prediction attributed to T2 in A17 is fabricated, so the test cannot discriminate between the stated theories, and its baseline is not the single professional range.
Duplicate theory presented as a rival, which gives a false appearance of comparing theories.
The decision rule is inconsistent: it has an unhandled 0–15% band, and A19 reverses the 15% condition.
A directly relevant observation (neumann-musicradar-upgrade, on upgrading to pro gear) was retrieved but never assessed.
The €20,000 / 12-week budget constraint is not present in the supplied case material and may be invented.

judgment.screen_reason: The episode is complete but contains several critical errors. Company marketing about tutorial videos is treated as demand evidence (A11, A12). Off-point and dated market data is labelled as support (A14). T2 is a copy of T1 (A9, A10), and the proposed test fabricates an opposing T2 prediction, so it cannot discriminate between the theories (A17). The recommendation is contradictory and unsupported (A18, A19). Any one of these errors would be enough to reject the trajectory.
